title: Episode 0 — The Desk Opens
summary: Before there's a case, there's a desk. Casey Quinn and Ray Sullivan open The Morning Blotter: who they are, what lands in your inbox every morning at 7:00 ET, how a case gets told evidence-first, the Sunday File and the mailbag — and why the hosts are AI-voiced.
notes_html:
Episode 0 — The Desk Opens. Before there's a case, there's a desk. Casey Quinn (the courts reporter — the voice of the victims) and Ray Sullivan (Bronx cop, homicide squad, twenty years an FBI profiler — the person who did it) open The Morning Blotter.

In this episode: the desk — who's sitting at it · the clock — what lands in your inbox every morning at seven (the brief, the top case, the Wire, the Case File, the Docket) · how we work — evidence first, and the rules we hold ourselves to · the Sunday File and the mailbag · the sign-off.

Subscribe free to the Morning Blotter email — the daily brief behind this program, every claim linked to its source — at morningblotter.com. The first edition lands in your inbox the morning it's ready.

Write to the desk: mailbag@morningblotter.com — questions about a case, how something works, what a word on the docket means. First names only on the air; we don't read tips about private people and we don't try cases in the mailbag.

The Morning Blotter is a produced program — Ray and Casey are AI-voiced storytellers. Every fact you hear comes from the sources linked in the daily brief at morningblotter.com. The reporting is checked by a human desk.
transcript:
[COLD OPEN]
CASEY: Every police station in America keeps a book. Used to be an actual book — bound, lined, a desk sergeant's handwriting: who came in, what happened to them, what time. They called it the blotter. And most of what gets called crime news? Starts as one line in that book, written by somebody who was tired… and did not care whether you'd ever read it.
RAY: I stood at that book. Twenty years old, midnights in the Four-Three, walking a collar up to the desk while the sergeant wrote it down. Name. Time. Charge. Whatever you walked in with — a wallet, a knife, a kid who wouldn't stop crying. Four lines. Nobody ever told me somebody'd read them.
CASEY: We care. Every morning at seven, this desk goes through the day's book — the arrests, the trials, the verdicts, the cases that are finally moving — and tells you what matters, and how we know. That's the whole idea. This is where it starts.

[THEME]
CASEY: This is The Morning Blotter. Episode zero — the desk opens. I'm Casey Quinn.
RAY: Ray Sullivan.
CASEY: Today you get the desk — who's sitting at it, how the show's built, and the rules we hold ourselves to. No cases yet.
RAY: And you get it once. That's the deal with an episode zero. We tell you who we are, we tell you how we do the job — and then we never make you sit through it again. After this? Cases.
CASEY: Hold us to it.

[DESK]
CASEY: First — the desk, who's sitting at it. I'll go first, because if I wait for Ray we'll be here till noon. I'm Casey Quinn, and I came up on the courts beat: years in the back row of courtrooms, learning that the story is never just the case file — it's the family in the second row, it's the name on the docket nobody says right. I'm the one who says the names. Ray. Your turn.
RAY: Yeah. Ray Sullivan. Woodlawn kid — that's the Bronx, top of the Bronx, where the Irish went when they got a little money and didn't want anybody to know about it. My father was on the job. His brother was on the job. So… nobody was surprised when I was on the job.
CASEY: On the job meaning —
RAY: The police. NYPD. Twenty years old, a sector car in the Four-Three — Soundview — midnights. You learn a lot at three in the morning. Mostly you learn who's lying to you. Which, at three in the morning? Everybody. Did ten years of that. Then I got the gold shield, went up to the squad. Homicide. Same job, except now the one person who could tell you what happened… is the one person who can't.
CASEY: And then the FBI came calling.
RAY: The Bureau, yeah. They wanted somebody who'd actually stood in the room — not read about the room. So I went down to Quantico and I spent twenty years as a profiler. Criminal analysis, they call it now. Same thing. Better letterhead.
CASEY: Which is what, exactly? For people who've only seen it on television.
RAY: People think it's a trick. It's not a trick. It's what a man did — read off the record, the way you'd read a ledger — and working out what kind of man does that. That's my lane on this show. The person who did it. Who he is, how he thinks, how his own behavior gets him caught. A profile tells you where to look. It doesn't tell you who did it. Big difference. That difference is the whole show.
CASEY: And now?
RAY: Now I'm retired. Supposedly. She calls at six in the morning with a docket.
CASEY: So when a detective on the news says the investigation is ongoing —
RAY: I know what that means. I've said it myself, more than once. It means one of two things. They've got nothing — and they're praying the phone rings. Or they've got everything, and the D.A. told them keep your mouth shut till the paperwork's done. Same six words. Two different worlds. Telling you which one you're looking at — that's what I'm here for.
CASEY: And the accent?
RAY: What accent.
CASEY: Okay.

[CLOCK]
CASEY: Next — the clock. Here's what lands in your inbox every morning at seven, seven days a week: first the brief, the cases that matter today, written like a magazine and sourced like a court filing — every claim links to where it came from: court records first, official statements second, reporters we trust third, and rumor? Never.
RAY: Never's a big word. Here's why she gets to say it. A rumor's the easiest thing in the world to print — it's free, it's fast, nobody has to sign it. A court filing costs somebody something. A man put his name on that. He can go to jail if it's a lie. That's why we tell you where a thing came from. It's not a footnote. It's the reason to believe it.
CASEY: Then, same hour, this program — ten to fifteen minutes of the two of us. We open with the top case, the one story you'd want if you only had time for one; then the Wire, three or four quick hits on what moved overnight — a verdict, a ruling, an arrest, a jury that's still out.
RAY: And the top case is the one that's actually news — not always the one with the best video. Some days the biggest thing that happened, happened in a courtroom with no cameras in it. Took forty seconds. A judge said yes, or a judge said no. That's the lead. The Wire? Short ones. Say it once, say it right. What moved, who moved it, what it means.
CASEY: Then the Case File — one case, told properly, start to finish, the way it actually happened. I carry the people it happened to, and that's where Ray takes it apart: the forensics, the procedure, the person who did it.
RAY: The way it can be shown to have happened.
CASEY: Fine — the way it can be shown to have happened. The things that sound like magic on television.
RAY: None of it's magic. Most of it's paperwork with a lab coat on. The DNA, the phone, the camera on the bodega across the street — every one of those is a piece of paper somebody had to go get, with a judge's name on the bottom. And then the part that's mine. What the man did, and what that says about him. Slowly. So you can see how it holds.
CASEY: And we close with the Docket — what's ahead: verdicts due, hearings, jury selections — so you know what to watch. Ten to fifteen minutes, start to finish.
RAY: Fifteen's a lot of talking.
CASEY: You just did three of them without stopping.

[HOW WE WORK]
CASEY: Okay. How we work. Ray — the rule, the one you gave me before we'd recorded a single word.
RAY: Evidence first.
CASEY: That's two words.
RAY: That's… that's the whole rule.
CASEY: No, come on. Unpack it. Not for me — for THEM.
RAY: Alright. Look. Everybody loves the moment somebody talks, right? The confession. The tape. The guy on the courthouse steps — you can stream it, you can clip it, everybody claps. Great. That's a story. That's NOT a case. A case is the slow part. The warrant. The timeline. The phone that puts a guy three blocks away when he swore up and down he was home. Where'd the gun go? Who saw the car? NOBODY claps for that. Nobody. But the slow part — that's what holds up in front of twelve strangers and a judge. So that's the order around here. What's shown. Then what's said. Then… what everybody thinks.
CASEY: And the people? The ones inside the case.
RAY: Depends which people. The one who did it — that's mine. Twenty years of asking what kind of person does this, and how does he get caught by what he does. The ones it happened to… that's her. And I'll tell you why. My whole career, the victim was a case number to me. Not proud of it. It's how you get through the tour. She's the one who's gonna make me say the name. And she's right. Somebody had to.
CASEY: My department. Okay, so here's what we hold ourselves to: victims get their names said RIGHT, and said more than once; anybody who's charged is the accused until a jury says otherwise — we don't skip ahead; nobody who hasn't been charged gets talked about like they have. And there's stuff we leave out, on purpose, because somebody's worst day is NOT entertainment.
RAY: That last one. Say that one again tomorrow. And the day after. I've stood in a lot of rooms on somebody's worst day. And there's ALWAYS — always — somebody outside who wants to sell it. We're not selling it. We tell you what happened, we tell you how we know, and the rest of it stays in the room. Where it belongs.
CASEY: Every day.
RAY: Every day. That's the job.

[SUNDAY MAILBAG]
CASEY: Two more things and we'll let you go. Sundays, the desk slows down — the Sunday File: one case, twenty-five to thirty-five minutes, told all the way through, the crime, the investigation, the courtroom, what's still unresolved. Some cases take more than one Sunday, and we'll say so.
RAY: Sundays are the good ones. Any case worth telling has three or four places where the whole thing turned on something small. A receipt. A phone call nobody returned. A witness who changed her mind. Sunday, we get to stand on those. That's the case the way the detectives lived it — not the way the headline had it.
CASEY: You would say that. Thirty minutes, and I ask you twelve questions.
RAY: Eleven too many.
CASEY: And the mailbag. Write to us — mailbag at morningblotter dot com — with questions about a case, about how something works, about what a word on the docket actually means. First names only on the air unless you tell us otherwise, and two things we won't do: read tips about private people, and try a case that hasn't been tried.
RAY: We don't try cases in the mailbag. Somebody writes in with a name and a theory — and look, I get it. I've had the theory. But a theory's the cheapest thing in the building. You wanna know how a thing works? Why the lab took nine months. Why the judge threw out the search. What a grand jury actually does. Write that. That, we'll answer all day.
CASEY: We don't try cases in the mailbag.

[SIGNOFF]
CASEY: That's the desk. It opens every morning at seven. The brief is free — subscribe at morningblotter dot com, and the first edition lands in your inbox the morning it's ready. One more thing, because we'd rather you hear it from us than discover it: Ray and I are AI-voiced. The reporting is checked by a human desk, against sources you can click and read for yourself. Nothing to discover, nothing to defend. Ray?
RAY: Sullivan. Last thing, and then she'll let you go. Everything you hear from me, you can check. That was the deal I made with her, and it's the deal we're making with you: you don't take my word for it. You take the record's word for it — and I read it to you in the order it happened. Evidence first.
CASEY: And the people, always. The Morning Blotter is a produced program — Ray and Casey are AI-voiced storytellers. Every fact you heard comes from the sources in today's brief at morningblotter.com.
